source_name: Slideworks (ex-McKinsey consultants), How McKinsey Consultants Make Presentations
quote: When you become a management consultant, one of the first things you are taught is that the title of a slide should always be an 'action title' that articulates the key takeaway or 'so-what' of the slide.
what: The action title is the slide title that states the key takeaway, or so-what, of the slide.
job: Let a busy reader get the slide's message without study of the slide body.
length: Two lines or less, same font size on all slides.
test: Read only the action titles in order: they must flow like a story and be readable on their own.

source_name: Penn State, How to Create an Assertion-Evidence Presentation (Michael Alley's assertion-evidence approach)
quote: Assertion-Evidence is a style of presentation in which a sentence headline states the main message of the slide-this is the “assertion” part.
what: The headline is one sentence, the assertion, that states the main message of the slide.
job: State the claim that the visual evidence on the slide then supports.
length: One sentence, no more than two lines.
test: Is the headline one full sentence that makes a claim, not a topic phrase?

source_name: Barbara Minto, The Pyramid Principle, Part 4 'Logic in Presentation' (as reviewed by StrategyU)
quote: For the text slides that remain, the rule is statements rather than captions. Her example is two words against four: “Sales outlook” versus “Sales outlook is favorable.”
what: The slide title is a statement of the point, not a caption that names a topic.
job: Leave the audience no room to assume a meaning other than the intended one.
test: Does the title make a statement ("Sales outlook is favorable"), not a caption ("Sales outlook")?

source_name: Antoine Buteau, Lessons from Gene Zelazny (Say It With Charts)
quote: Use a title that conveys the chart’s takeaway rather than merely naming the data; Zelazny’s chart portfolio includes message titles for its examples.
what: A message title conveys the chart's takeaway instead of only naming the data.
job: Tell the audience what to learn from the chart.
test: Does the title state a takeaway, or does it only name the data?

source_name: Office for National Statistics (ONS) Digital Blog, Say what you see: the way we write chart titles is changing
quote: We should be aiming to have chart titles that sum up the main message shown in the chart in 10 words or less.
what: A chart title sums up the main message that the chart shows.
job: Prime the reader to see the intended trend and avoid misinterpretation.
test: Does the title state the chart's main message in 10 words or less?

source_name: Slideworks (ex-McKinsey consultants), How McKinsey Consultants Make Presentations
quote: Subheadings are meant to give a clear summary of the data used to prove the insight in the action title, or alternatively add some nuance to the main takeaway. Keep it crisp and short.
what: The subheading summarises the data that proves the action title, or adds nuance to it.
job: Tell the reader what data the slide uses to prove the title.
length: Crisp and short, e.g. "Sales of personal luxury goods, US Market, $ billions".
test: Does the subheading name the data used to prove the title's insight?

source_name: The Analyst Academy, Takeaway Boxes: When To Use Them And When To Avoid Them
quote: They’re usually more specific than the title and they tell us where to look to better understand the main message of the slide.
what: The subtitle is a more specific line under the title that directs attention.
job: Show the audience where to look to understand the title's message.
test: Is the subtitle more specific than the title, and does it point to the key part of the slide?

source_name: Office for National Statistics (ONS) Digital Blog, Say what you see: the way we write chart titles is changing
quote: This doesn’t mean we want to lose the statistical information, this approach still includes a short subtitle outlining the data, geography and time period.
what: The subtitle is a short line that gives the chart's data, geography and time period.
job: Keep the statistical information that the message title leaves out.
test: Does the subtitle state the data, the geography and the time period?

source_name: Mark Nold, The Anatomy of a Slide: The Basics
quote: Sits below the Headline and summarises the content of the slide below;
what: The subheading sits below the headline and summarises the content of the slide.
job: Explain clearly and quickly the point the data below makes.
test: Does it summarise the data below and the conclusion, with no new data and no emotive language?

source_name: PPT PowerTools, The anatomy of a consulting slide
quote: As seen above, the subtitle provides additional context and insights to complement a descriptive title. Its purpose is to deepen the audience’s understanding of the slide’s focus, ensuring clarity and precision.
what: The subtitle adds context and insight to complement a descriptive title.
job: Deepen the audience's understanding of the slide's focus.
test: If the title is already an action title, omit the subtitle; the source says it can dilute the impact.

source_name: Management Consulted, Consulting Slide Deck: Do's and Don'ts
quote: Charts should include key takeaways. While great graphics should speak for themselves, skilled consultants include a summary, or key takeaway, from the chart on the slide.
what: A key takeaway is a short summary, on the slide, of what the chart shows.
job: State the key insight that the chart represents, next to the chart.
test: Is there a stated insight beside the chart, or must the reader infer it?

source_name: StrategyU, The 14 Slide Layouts That Consulting Firms Use for Everything
quote: A chart takes up the left two-thirds of the slide. The right third holds a text box with the takeaway or recommendation. A callout arrow or highlight on the chart draws the eye to the specific data point that matters.
what: A takeaway text box sits beside the chart, with callouts that mark the data it refers to.
job: Draw the eye to the specific data point that supports the insight.
test: Does each callout point to a specific bar, line or data point, not to the chart in general?

source_name: Penn State, How to Create an Assertion-Evidence Presentation (Michael Alley's assertion-evidence approach)
quote: If necessary, add a call-out (words or phrases used to clarify images) to improve the viewer’s understanding of the visual evidence.
what: A call-out is a word or phrase placed on the visual to clarify it.
job: Improve the viewer's understanding of the visual evidence.
length: One or two call-outs per slide; three or more clutter the slide.
test: Are there two call-outs or fewer, and does each clarify the visual?

source_name: Slideworks (ex-McKinsey consultants), How McKinsey Consultants Make Presentations
quote: Add call-outs, highlights or similar wherever it makes sense to make the so-what of that visual more clear.
what: Call-outs and highlights are marks on a visual that make its so-what clear.
job: Make the so-what of the visual clearer.
test: Does each call-out make the visual's so-what clearer?

source_name: Slideworks (ex-McKinsey consultants), How McKinsey Consultants Make Presentations
quote: The slide's main insight, articulated in the action title, should be supported by all relevant information presented in the simplest possible way.
what: The slide body is the data that proves the insight stated in the action title.
job: Support the title's insight with relevant information in the simplest possible way.
test: Remove all facts and figures that do not directly support the insight in the title.

source_name: Michael Alley, assertion-evidence.com (Assertion-Evidence Approach)
quote: In this approach, you build your presentations on succinct messages (assertions), rather than phrase topics. Moreover, to support those messages, you provide visual evidence rather than bulleted lists.
what: The slide body is visual evidence that supports the assertion in the headline.
job: Support the headline's message with visual evidence, not a bulleted list.
test: Is the body visual evidence (chart, photo, diagram), not a bulleted list?

source_name: Barbara Minto, The Pyramid Principle, Part 4 'Logic in Presentation' (as reviewed by StrategyU)
quote: Work out what question the chart is answering. Put the answer in the title. Choose the chart form last, once you know what it has to show.
what: The exhibit answers one question, and its answer goes in the title.
job: Show the answer that the title states.
test: Did you choose the chart form only after you knew the question and its answer?

source_name: Antoine Buteau, Lessons from Gene Zelazny (Say It With Charts)
quote: Zelazny’s chart method begins with the message, then identifies the comparison and selects the chart form.
what: The chart is the form selected to express the message and its comparison type.
job: Express the comparison behind the message in a fitting chart form.
test: Name the comparison (component, item, time series, frequency distribution, correlation) before you pick the chart form.

source_name: The Analyst Academy, Takeaway Boxes: When To Use Them And When To Avoid Them
quote: Consulting firms love to use takeaway boxes. That small rectangular box of text at the bottom of a slide sometimes also called a kicker.
what: The takeaway box, or kicker, is a small box of text at the bottom of the slide.
job: Call out a second-order insight that supports the title, or set up the next slide.
test: It is not the main takeaway (that is the title), adds no new information, and appears on fewer than 20% of slides.

source_name: Slideworks (ex-McKinsey consultants), How to Write Key Takeaway Slides
quote: A small rectangular box of text at the bottom of a slide, sometimes also called a ‘kicker box’.
what: A key takeaway box, or kicker box, is a small text box at the bottom of one slide.
job: Highlight a granular point on that one slide, not the whole presentation.
test: Does the box relate only to this slide, not to the whole presentation?

source_name: Consultant's Mind, Better PowerPoint: 6 Ways to Make Your Point
quote: Emphasize your point by using different colors, or using a call-out box (sometimes called “kicker box”) to reiterate the point at the bottom of the slide
what: A kicker box is a call-out box at the bottom of the slide.
job: Reiterate the slide's point so that it answers "What's the so what?"
test: If a manager asks "What's the so what?", does the kicker give the answer?

source_name: PPT PowerTools, The anatomy of a consulting slide
quote: The footnote is a vital component of the slide, providing the foundation for its credibility. It is used to cite sources, offer clarifications, or include disclaimers, ensuring transparency and professionalism.
what: The footnote cites sources and gives clarifications or disclaimers for the slide.
job: Give the slide its credibility through transparent sources.
length: Do not overwhelm it with excessive detail.
test: Is all data on the slide backed by a source citation in a standard format?

source_name: Ampler, Insert and update footnotes in PowerPoint
quote: Every data point and non-obvious claim carries a footnote - Source: for the provenance of data, Note: for methodology, assumptions, or definitions.
what: Footnotes are Source: lines for data provenance and Note: lines for method or definitions.
job: Make the analysis defensible in senior review.
length: Short: a source or a caveat, not a paragraph; a citation, not a sentence.
test: Does every data point and non-obvious claim have a Source: or Note: footnote?

source_name: Consultport, Consulting Presentation Checklist: Make Sure to Include These 7 Elements
quote: Now, on the bottom left corner, consulting slides should include the source and date.
what: The source and date line sits in the bottom left corner of the slide.
job: Name who made the slide and where its data comes from.
test: Does the bottom left corner show the source and date, with footnotes for extra remarks?

source_name: Mark Nold, The Anatomy of a Slide: The Basics
quote: Use for sources or citations. Can be used for qualifiers that must accompany the data;
what: Footnotes hold sources, citations and qualifiers that must go with the data.
job: Increase transparency and the reader's trust in the data.
test: Use one consistent format: "Source Organisation Name (Date). Document Name or URL."

source_name: Slideworks (ex-McKinsey consultants), How McKinsey Consultants Make Presentations
quote: Each slide should also have a slide number and a source in the bottom section that provides the source of the data used.
what: The source line in the bottom section gives the source of the data used.
job: Show where the slide's data comes from.
test: Does every slide have a source and a slide number in the bottom section?
